species.habitat: Rocky points, lava benches, channel edges, sandy flats near structure
species.regulations: No statewide bag or size limit; confirm current rules at DLNR.Hawaii.gov
identification_features: Steep, nearly vertical forehead in large adults
Deep, laterally compressed silver body
Dark spots or mottled blotches on fish over 20 lbs
Deeply forked lunate tail with dark upper lobe
Hard scutes along posterior lateral line
catch_methods: Shore casting — surface lures (pencil poppers, stickbaits, GT Ice Cream)
Live bait — akule, papio, or small reef fish
Jigging vertically near structure drop-offs
Fly fishing with 9–12 wt rod and large saltwater streamers
best_spots: Ka Lae / South Point (strong current, large fish)
Anaehoomalu Bay channel and reef edge
species.preparation: Firm, white, mild flesh. Bleed immediately after catch for best quality. Excellent sashimi, grilled fillets, or pan-fried. Larger fish (>20 lbs) are better smoked or cooked than eaten raw.

species.habitat: Sandy beaches, small bays, tidal flats, shallow reef edges
species.regulations: Juvenile form of multiple ulua/trevally species. No statewide bag limit; check DLNR for current rules.
identification_features: Smaller body than ulua, typically under 10 lbs
Silver sides often with faint yellow tinge
Dark spot near pectoral fin base on many species
Omilu (bluefin trevally) has vivid blue fins and spotted body
catch_methods: Light tackle with small plugs, spoons, or jigs
Live bait or cut bait on sandy bottoms
Cast-and-retrieve from beach or pier
best_spots: Puako tide pools and reef edge
Any sandy bay along the Kohala coast
species.preparation: Mild white flesh. Pan-fry, grill, or steam whole. Good sashimi when very fresh. Bleed promptly after catch.

species.habitat: Sandy shorelines, surf zones, nearshore sand flats
species.regulations: REGULATED: Minimum size 11 inches total length. Bag limit 10 fish/day. No moi fishing April 1–July 31 (spawning season) in some areas. Verify current DLNR rules before fishing.
identification_features: Silvery body with faint diagonal stripes
Distinctive thread-like pectoral fin rays extending forward
Blunt snout, inferior mouth (faces down for bottom feeding)
Forked tail; typically 1–5 lbs
catch_methods: Light surf tackle with small hooks and sand crabs (ohiki) as bait
Slide baiting along sandy beaches
Small flies or soft plastics in the surf
best_spots: Any long sandy beach along the Kohala coast
species.preparation: Sweet, delicate white flesh — historically a royal (kapu) fish. Grill whole, steam, or pan-fry. Minimal seasoning needed. Excellent sashimi.
species.safety_note: REGULATED SPECIES: Check current DLNR seasons and size/bag limits before harvesting.

species.habitat: Coral reef edges, rocky bottoms, sandy areas adjacent to reef
species.depth_range: 2–100 m; commonly taken from shore at 5–15 m
species.best_season: Year-round; better at dusk and night
species.regulations: No statewide bag or size limit; confirm at DLNR.Hawaii.gov
identification_features: Large eyes (characteristic feature)
Silvery-white body, often with faint brownish bars
Robust body with small mouth
Can change color pattern rapidly
catch_methods: Bottom fishing with cut bait (urchin, crab, small fish) near reef
Night fishing from rocky shorelines and piers
Small circle hooks with light leader near structure
best_spots: Any rocky shoreline adjacent to reef
species.preparation: Mild, white, firm flesh. Grill, steam, or bake whole. Popular for stew (lawalu style). Remove tough outer skin for fillets.

species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, mixed sand-rubble near reef, tide pools
species.regulations: No statewide bag or size limit; confirm at DLNR.Hawaii.gov. Weke pueo (M. pfluegeri) reported to cause nightmares — avoid or use caution.
identification_features: Elongated body with two distinctive chin barbels
Yellowfin weke: yellow lateral stripe, yellow fins
Bandtail weke: white body with distinct black tail band
Often seen in small groups over sand, tilting nose-down to forage
catch_methods: Light bottom fishing with small hooks, shrimp, or worm bait
Netting in schools over sandy shallows
Spearfishing while cruising sandy bottom
species.preparation: Light, sweet flesh. Grill whole, steam, or pan-fry. Common in traditional Hawaiian plate lunches. Salt-brine before cooking enhances flavor.
species.safety_note: Weke pueo (M. pfluegeri) may cause hallucinogenic nightmares — identified by darker coloration and blunter head. Confirm species before eating at night.

species.habitat: Shallow reef caves, crevices, coral heads; nocturnal
species.regulations: No statewide bag or size limit; confirm at DLNR.Hawaii.gov
identification_features: Bright red body with white or silver horizontal stripes
Large eyes (adapted for nocturnal feeding)
Spiny dorsal fin; sharp preopercle spine
Relatively small fish, rarely over 1 lb
catch_methods: Night fishing from rocks with small hooks and shrimp bait
Small lures around reef crevices at dusk
Spearfishing in caves and under ledges at night
best_spots: Any rocky shoreline with reef caves at night
Puako and Anaehoomalu reef edges at night
species.preparation: Small but flavorful. Pan-fry or deep-fry whole. Good in fish soup or miso soup. Bones are manageable in small fish.
species.safety_note: Handle carefully — dorsal fin spines and preopercle spine are sharp.

species.habitat: Open nearshore waters, often in large schools near surface; bays and harbors
species.best_season: Year-round; watch for birds diving to locate schools
species.regulations: No statewide bag or size limit; confirm at DLNR.Hawaii.gov
identification_features: Large eyes relative to body size
Silvery elongated body with greenish back
Small fish in schools of hundreds to thousands
Scutes along posterior lateral line
catch_methods: Cast net (upena) when schools are spotted near surface
Sabiki rigs (multiple small hooks) drifted through schools
Used as live bait for ulua and other large predators
best_spots: Watch for diving seabirds (noio, wedge-tailed shearwater) indicating schools
species.preparation: Rich, oily fish similar to mackerel. Traditional preparation: salt-dried (paakai), grilled whole, or fermented. Excellent smoked. Cook immediately or preserve — oily flesh spoils quickly.
species.safety_note: Oily flesh spoils faster than white-fish species. Ice or preserve immediately.

species.habitat: Open nearshore and offshore waters; forms large midwater schools
species.depth_range: Surface to 100 m; commonly caught nearshore
species.regulations: No statewide bag or size limit; confirm at DLNR.Hawaii.gov
identification_features: Slender, elongated body, more cylindrical than akule
Metallic blue-green back, silver sides
Single small finlet behind dorsal and anal fins
Smaller mouth than akule; less prominent eyes
catch_methods: Cast net (upena) near surface schools
Sabiki rigs or small feather jigs
Traditional opelu trap (hokeo) used in deeper water
best_spots: Offshore areas along the Kona coast
species.preparation: Similar to akule — rich and oily. Excellent grilled whole, salt-dried, or smoked. Traditional Hawaiian preparation includes fermenting with salt and seaweed.
species.safety_note: Ice quickly after catch; oily fish spoils fast.

species.habitat: Coral reefs, rocky reef areas with algae growth
species.avg_size: 2–10 lbs; large terminal-phase males up to 30 lbs
species.regulations: No statewide bag or size limit, but spearfishing regulations apply. No spearfishing in designated Marine Life Conservation Districts (MLCDs). Check area-specific rules.
identification_features: Fused beak-like teeth (parrot beak) for scraping algae from coral
Initial phase: drab brown/red; terminal phase: brilliant blue, green, and pink
Produces mucus cocoon when sleeping
Grinding sound audible underwater when feeding
catch_methods: Spearfishing on freedive or SCUBA near reef
Spearguns or Hawaiian slings; often targeted at night when sleeping
Not typically caught by hook-and-line
best_spots: Reefs along the Kona coast outside MLCDs
species.preparation: White, mild flesh. Good grilled, steamed, or in stew. Terminal-phase males (blue/green) are most commonly targeted for size. Scale carefully.
species.safety_note: Do NOT spearfish in Marine Life Conservation Districts (Kahaluu, Lapakahi, Waialea, Old Kona Airport, Kona Coast SP). Know your location before diving.

species.habitat: Rocky shorelines, shallow reef flats, tide pools, surge zones
species.depth_range: Shoreline to 15 m; very common in knee-deep water
species.regulations: No statewide bag or size limit; confirm at DLNR.Hawaii.gov. Cannot spear in MLCDs.
identification_features: White-gray body with 5–6 distinct black vertical bars (convict stripes)
Small fish, rarely over 0.5 lbs
Retractable sharp spine at base of tail
Moves in large grazing schools across reef flats
catch_methods: Spearfishing with short spear or pole spear in shallows
Netting with fine-mesh net in surge zones
Hook-and-line with very small hooks and seaweed bait (rarely used)
best_spots: Any rocky shoreline with reef flat
species.preparation: Small but flavorful. Often dried (dried manini are a traditional snack). Pan-fry whole, deep-fry, or steam. Gut promptly after catch.
species.safety_note: Sharp caudal spine — handle carefully, grab fish from behind the head.

species.habitat: Rocky reefs, surge zones, areas with encrusting algae
species.regulations: No statewide bag or size limit. No spearfishing in MLCDs.
identification_features: Brown/olive body with faint horizontal lines
Distinctive yellow-gold ring around each eye
Oval body; small mouth with comb-like teeth for scraping algae
Sharp spine at base of tail (caudal peduncle)
catch_methods: Spearfishing on reef flats and surge zones
Pole spear in shallows
best_spots: Rocky reef areas along Kona and Kohala coasts
species.preparation: Mild white flesh. Pan-fry, grill, or steam. Often prepared whole. Good in soup. Very fresh fish can be used in poke.

species.scientific_name: Cellana exarata / C. sandwicensis / C. talcosa
species.habitat: Rocky shoreline — wave-splash zone to intertidal zone; high-energy lava bench areas preferred
species.best_season: Year-round; best when surf is 2 ft or less
species.avg_size: 1–3 inch shell diameter; harvest only over 1.25 inches
species.regulations: Minimum size 1.25 inches (3.18 cm) shell length. Bag limit 100 per person per day. Do not harvest in Marine Life Conservation Districts.
identification_features: Conical limpet shell, gray-white exterior, gray-brown interior
Three species: ko'ele (black foot, highest zone), alinalina (yellow foot, mid zone), makaiauli (white foot, lowest zone)
Firmly attached to lava rock — requires flat blade to pry loose
Foot muscle is the edible part
catch_methods: Pry from rocks with flat-bladed opihi knife or thin putty knife
Approach carefully and remove swiftly — animal retracts if it detects vibration
Work during low tide on calm days only
Never harvest from extremely high-danger wave zones
best_spots: Remote lava bench areas along Kohala coast
Any accessible lava bench with wave splash during calm weather
species.preparation: Traditionally eaten raw on the half shell with Hawaiian salt. Can be lightly cooked on the half shell over coals. Drizzle with sesame oil and shoyu. Do not overcook — turns rubbery.
species.safety_note: SERIOUS DANGER: Opihi picking is one of the most dangerous activities on Hawaii's shores. Rogue waves appear without warning on lava benches. Never turn your back to the ocean. Do not pick during high surf. People die every year harvesting opihi.

species.scientific_name: Caulerpa racemosa / Gracilaria coronopifolia / Asparagopsis taxiformis
species.habitat: Intertidal and shallow subtidal reef flats, tide pools, nearshore rocky areas
species.best_season: Year-round; some species more abundant seasonally
species.edibility_rating: Excellent — essential in traditional Hawaiian diet
species.regulations: Non-commercial harvest generally unrestricted. Do not harvest in MLCDs. Respect any posted signs.
identification_features: Limu kohu (Asparagopsis taxiformis): reddish, feathery, strong pungent aroma — premium sashimi limu
Limu wawae'iole (Caulerpa racemosa): green, grape-like clusters, mild flavor
Limu ele'ele (Enteromorpha spp.): thin green sheets, mild flavor, common
Avoid limu with unusual smell or dark slime — may indicate pollution
catch_methods: Hand-pick from rocks and reef flats during low tide
Submerge hands in tide pools to feel for limu among rocks
Bring mesh bag for collection and rinsing
best_spots: Tide pools along Kona and Kohala coasts
Shallow reef areas at low tide
species.preparation: Rinse thoroughly in fresh water. Limu kohu: serve fresh with poke or sashimi. Limu wawae'iole: use fresh in poke, salads, or as garnish. Most edible limu can be lightly pickled (namasu style) with rice vinegar.
species.safety_note: Harvest only from areas away from runoff and sewage outfalls. Never harvest limu that smells strongly of decay or petroleum.

species.habitat: Shallow reef flats, rocky bottoms, wave-exposed areas; hides in crevices during day
species.best_season: Year-round; roe quality best in spring and summer
species.regulations: No statewide bag or size limit; confirm at DLNR.Hawaii.gov
identification_features: Extremely long, hollow, sharp black spines (up to 12 inches)
Round purple-black to dark brown test (shell)
Common on reef flats, often in clusters
Spines can penetrate wetsuit — approach with extreme caution
catch_methods: Hand-pick with thick gloves or grab with tongs
Cut test in half with knife to access roe (roe is on inner walls)
Harvest carefully — spines break off and are painful to remove
best_spots: Shallow reef flats along Kona coast
species.preparation: Roe (called ina): scoop out yellow or orange roe from inside the test. Eat fresh with shoyu, or use in poke. Traditional Hawaiian preparation with Hawaiian salt and limu. Used to flavor soups and rice.
species.safety_note: PAINFUL SPINES: Long spines easily penetrate skin and break off. Wear thick gloves. If stung, remove spine fragments and soak in hot water. Spines may require medical removal. Never step on or near wana barefoot.

species.habitat: Rocky reefs, lava ledges, crevices; hides during day, forages at night
species.depth_range: Shallow shoreline to 60 m; accessible from shore at night in shallows
species.regulations: SEASONAL CLOSURE: May 1–August 31. Minimum carapace length 3.25 inches. Bag limit 6 per person per day. No egg-bearing females. Verify current DLNR rules.
identification_features: Spiny body without claws (spiny lobster)
Banded orange-brown and white tail
Long, spiny antennae (longer than body)
Distinctive white spots on body segments
Ula poni (P. penicillatus) is more spotted and slightly different
catch_methods: Night snorkeling or freediving with flashlight along rocky shoreline
Grab from behind — approach slowly and grab across the carapace
Hoop nets from piers at night with fish bait
Do NOT use SCUBA or slurp guns for lobster
best_spots: Rocky shorelines along Kohala and Kona coasts at night
Reef edges accessible by snorkel at night
species.preparation: Boil or steam live (10–12 min for a 2 lb lobster). Grill split in half with butter and garlic. Meat is sweet and firm. Excellent chilled with citrus.
species.safety_note: SEASONAL CLOSURE May 1–August 31. Minimum carapace 3.25 inches. No egg-bearing females. Violations carry significant fines under Hawaii law.
